record.question:
An insurer runs web servers behind a load balancer. Its security policy requires the TLS private key to be generated and used inside company-controlled dedicated HSMs, with key extraction disabled. Application logs must survive instance termination, and only an audit role may read and decrypt the archived logs.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Store the TLS private key on encrypted EBS volumes attached to the web servers. Archive logs in S3 with SSE-KMS and restrict access to the audit role.

Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Download the TLS private key from a restricted S3 bucket at server startup. Archive logs in S3 with SSE-S3 and allow all server administrators to read them.
Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Use a non-extractable key in CloudHSM for TLS private-key operations. Store logs only on encrypted EC2 instance-store volumes.

Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Use a non-extractable key in a multi-AZ CloudHSM cluster for TLS private-key operations. Archive logs in S3 with SSE-KMS and restrict object reads and key decryption to the audit role.

explanation.text:
Choose <<4>>. The web servers terminate TLS while delegating supported private-key operations to CloudHSM. The Network Load Balancer uses a TCP listener so it passes the TLS session through. Generating the key inside the HSM and marking it non-extractable establishes the required key boundary. S3 provides durable log storage, and S3 authorization plus the KMS key policy restrict who can obtain plaintext archives.

<<1>> places usable private-key material on the servers, even though the disks are encrypted. <<2>> likewise copies the key out of an HSM boundary; SSE-S3 does not prevent permitted S3 readers from receiving decrypted logs. <<3>> protects the TLS key but instance store is not durable across termination.

Key custody and data-read authorization are separate controls. An HSM can protect a key from extraction while an authorized application still invokes it. Configure HSM client access, resilient HSM placement and least-privilege log-writer permissions; do not grant the writers log-read access merely because they upload logs.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudHSM TLS offload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/ssl-offload.html), [CloudHSM key attributes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/key-attribute-table.html), [S3 SSE-KMS permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html). [CloudHSM availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/cluster-high-availability-load-balancing.html).

diagram_alt: TLS key operations stay inside CloudHSM; separate S3 and KMS checks control archived-log reads.

sources.supports: Compatible web servers delegate TLS private-key cryptographic operations to CloudHSM.
Extractable and never-extractable attributes govern whether HSM key material can be exported.
SSE-KMS downloads require KMS decryption permission in addition to S3 access.
Multiple HSMs in separate AZs provide redundant key operations and synchronized keys.

editorial_notes: Made dedicated-HSM custody, non-extractability, durable logs and audit-role access explicit so ACM alone is not an equally valid answer.
Clarified CloudHSM offload covers private-key operations rather than every byte of TLS traffic.
